article.title: Don't Ask AI to Predict the Market. Ask It to Break Your Strategy
article.preview_text: Most people use Claude or GPT in trading the same way: paste a chart, ask "buy or sell?". That is the weakest use. The better one is a hostile reviewer for your own backtest. Many practitioners

blocks.text: Most people use Claude or GPT in trading the same way: paste a chart, ask "buy or sell?". That is the weakest use. The better one is a hostile reviewer for your own backtest. Many practitioners already describe AI this way: an engineering assistant for code, review and challenging assumptions, not a generator of buy and sell calls.
To see what that looks like, I built a market where nothing can earn money, planted three common bugs in a simple strategy, and measured how much each one lies.
The market is pure noise: 2,520 days with 1% daily volatility. The strategy is a 2/10 moving-average crossover with a 0.05% cost per side. Every number below is an average of 40 runs.
The honest version scored a Sharpe of −0.22. That is the correct answer for a market with nothing in it, and it is the number every buggy version should be compared to.

If the signal uses today's close and the trade earns today's return, the bot trades on information it did not have. Without the one-day shift, the same strategy scored a Sharpe of 3.30. One missing line produced the whole result.

Language models carry a version of this problem inside them. Research on ChatGPT-style trading signals notes that backtests are hard to trust when the model was trained on data that already contains the outcome.

The strategy flips position about 36 times a year. With costs ignored, its Sharpe was 0.00. With 0.05% per side it was −0.22, and with costs doubled it fell to −0.43. Fast strategies live or die on costs, and AI-written code often leaves them out unless you ask.

I tested 30 combinations of fast and slow windows and kept the best one. It showed a Sharpe of 0.45 on the history. On fresh data with costs it scored 0.05. Asking an AI to "optimize the parameters" is a request to do exactly this.

Give the model your code and your results, and tell it what job to do. One trader's tip is to make the model ask questions before it gives feedback, instead of praising the first draft. Run the review in a separate conversation from the one that wrote the code, because a model that built the strategy tends to defend it.
Check the data. A model reads your code, not your feed. It cannot see a survivor-only universe unless you tell it where the tickers came from.
Replace the test. Ask it to find the problem, then verify with your own run: shift the signal, double the costs, rerun on new data.
Know its own training window. If you use a model to judge past dates, test it only after its cutoff.
The result of this workflow is not a better prediction. It is fewer lies in your backtest.

data.markdown:
```plaintext
You are a skeptical quant reviewer. Do not improve my strategy.
Your only job is to find reasons the result is fake.
Read the code below and list, in order of severity:
1. Any place a signal could use data from after the decision time.
2. Any missing costs, slippage or fill assumptions.
3. How many versions or parameters were tried, and what that does to the result.
4. Whether the universe contains only survivors.
5. What I should run next to disprove this result.
Quote the exact line for each problem. If you find nothing, say what
you could not check.
```
